# Research notes on Ezekiel 10

Here are verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 10, each with its source page. Two gaps first. I didn't find any Catholic or Orthodox material, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, on this chapter, so those are left out. And I didn't find whole Protestant traditions splitting over any verse here. The differences I did find are between individual teachers, and Section 2 lists them.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- **Guzik:** The throne is described as in 1:26, but this time Ezekiel doesn't mention the man on it. Yet the person on the throne is *implied*, from the **He** who **spoke to the man clothed with linen**. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-10/
- **Guzik, quoting Block:** The cherubim are the living heavenly beings that the statues in the inner sanctuary only pictured. They came to carry God's visible glory out of the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-10/
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** To avoid giving too great prominence in this appearance of Jehovah to the bodily or human form, Ezekiel does not speak even here of the form of Jehovah, but simply of His throne. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-1.htm
- **Calvin:** The throne sits above the cherubim because the angels are not independent, but are so subject to God that they always depend upon his nod. He also says the throne is placed above the sky so the prophet would not imagine anything earthly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-10.html
- **Benson:** The repetition of the vision here signified that the heavy and terrible judgments of God were drawing nearer and nearer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-1.htm
- **Precept Austin:** The figure in glory is "almost certainly" Christ before his incarnation. The sapphire matches the pavement under God's feet in Exodus 24:10. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_101-14

**v. 2:**
- **Ellicott:** In chapter 9 the man in linen did a work of mercy, marking the faithful. Now he becomes the agent of judgment, in the same way that blessings turn to curses when people abuse them. The "coals of fire," the symbols of Divine wrath, are represented as "between the cherubim." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-2.htm
- **Ellicott:** 2 Kings 25:9 and 2 Chronicles 36:19 show that the Temple and city were actually burned by the Chaldæans. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-10.html
- **Guzik:** The fire comes *from the throne and glory of God itself*. He quotes Taylor: Jerusalem would be treated like Sodom and Gomorrah. He quotes Feinberg: in Isaiah 6 the coals cleansed the prophet, but here they destroy the wicked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-10/
- **JFB:** This fire is not taken from the altar, where peace was made with God. It comes from the wheels, which stand for God's providence, so the judgment does not fall by chance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-2.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** The word for "wheelwork" (*galgal*) is a collective word meaning "whirling." It is also used for whirlwinds and chariot wheels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-2.htm
- **NET note:** The Hebrew text has the singular "cherub." The ancient versions have the plural, and a copying slip probably dropped the ending. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=10

**v. 3:**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** In Hebrew usage the "right side" means the south. The cherubim should be pictured near the altar, then moving to its south side. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-1.htm
- **Guzik:** The south is the opposite side from where the angels of judgment began their work (9:1–2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-10/
- **JFB:** The cloud is an emblem of God's displeasure; as the "glory" or "brightness" ( Eze 10:4 ) typifies His majesty and clearness in judgment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eze/Eze_010.cfm

**v. 4:**
- **Ellicott:** Here the singular "cherub" may mean the cherubim over the mercy seat. In that case the Presence is leaving the Holy of Holies preparatory to leaving it altogether. The scene is a stark contrast with Exodus 40 and 1 Kings 8, when God first took up residence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-10.html
- **Barnes:** This repeats 9:3. Ezekiel 10:4-6 describe what had occurred before the "man went in" Ezekiel 10:3. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-4.htm
- **Calvin:** The temple grew dark while the threshold, a place everyone could see, became bright. The point is that God, having left his temple, now appeared outside it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/10-4.html
- **JFB:** The temple, once filled with brightness, is now darkened with cloud. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eze/Eze_010.cfm
- **Benson:** The glory paused to show God's unwillingness to leave his people, and give them time to return to him. Guzik quotes Poole making the same point. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-4.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The brilliant splendour is a symbol of the light of the divine grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-1.htm

**v. 5:**
- **Benson:** The sound was like the sound of loud thunder. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-4.htm
- **Guzik, quoting Block:** The noise of the wings gives an impression of restlessness, an eagerness to be gone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-10/
- **NET note:** The name "El Shaddai" is usually rendered "God Almighty," mainly because of Jerome's Latin translation. Its meaning is much debated. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=10

**vv. 6–7:**
- **Guzik:** The man doesn't take the fire himself; a cherub hands it to him. He quotes Taylor: perhaps even this messenger had to keep his distance from God's throne. He quotes Morgan: God's fire will harm nothing save that which is evil. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-10/
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The words "and he went out" show that the man scattered the coals over the city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-2.htm

**v. 8:**
- **NET note:** The word translated "form" is normally used for building plans, such as the pattern of the tabernacle or temple. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=10
- **Guzik:** The hands explain how the cherub could pass the fire. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-10/

**v. 9:**
- **NET note:** The Hebrew says "Tarshish stone," and its meaning is uncertain. Versions translate it topaz, beryl, chrysolite or jasper. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=10
- **Poole:** The wheels stand for the turning events of this world, unstable but governed by a sure wisdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-9.htm

**v. 10:**
- **JFB:** The wheels cross each other at right angles, so the whole can move in any of four directions. God's doings, however involved they seem to us, cohere, so that lower causes subserve the higher. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-10.htm
- **Calvin:** "Wheel within wheel" admits that God's works confuse us, but the eyes in v. 12 correct that impression. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-10.html
- **NET note, citing Allen:** Some picture wheels inside each other; others picture a globe made of two wheels at right angles. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=10

**v. 11:**
- **JFB:** With a face toward every direction, the creatures never needed to turn. The wheels were not guided by some external adventitious impetus, but by some secret divine impulse of the cherubim themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-11.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** "The head" means the front wheel, which starts the motion and sets the direction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-13.htm
- **NET note:** Many interpreters think each cherub's human face was the one looking forward. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=10

**v. 12:**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** This is new: in 1:18 only the wheel rims had eyes, but Here the eyes are everywhere. The prophet receives a new impression of the all-seeing eye of Jehovah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-12.htm
- **Poole:** "Body" is figurative, since angels don't have flesh. The eyes mean wisdom, foresight, watchfulness, and diligence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-12.htm
- **Guzik:** This matches the cherubim of Revelation 4:6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-10/

**v. 13:**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** Someone called out to the wheels, "Whirl!" This was the signal to start moving, and Theodoret explained it the same way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-18.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The singular word may best be rendered "the chariot." He recognized that as the right name of the whole mysterious and complex form. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-13.htm

**v. 14:**
This verse is the main puzzle of the chapter. In 1:10 the first face was an ox; here it is a cherub.
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The prophet names the face each creature turned toward him. Ezekiel now sees this as "emphatically the cherubic form." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-14.htm
- **Barnes, Dummelow and Cambridge:** The difference comes from where Ezekiel was standing as the chariot was about to move east. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-14.htm and https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-10.html
- **Clarke:** A cherub must have had the likeness of an ox, at least in its head. כרוב kerub never occurs as a verb; and its meaning cannot be precisely ascertained. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/10-14.html
- **JFB, against Clarke:** The chief of the four cherubic forms was not the ox, but man. So "cherub" cannot simply mean "ox." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-14.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** The ox face was dropped because the face of the cherub had been most abused by the worship of an ox. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_010.cfm
- **Calvin:** He rejects both "it looked like an ox from far away" and "cherub means ox." In his view the second vision really was different, so that the prophet would know these creatures were angels. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom22.v.xiv.html
- **Ellicott:** Since v. 22 says the faces were the same, the variation is only in the description, and not in the thing described. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-10.html

**v. 15:**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The recognition is complete. It moves wheels and wings and cherubim, all as by one harmonious impulse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-15.htm
- **Calvin:** God repeats the vision because faith grows as God speaks to us again and again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-10.html

**vv. 16–17:**
- **Benson:** There is a perfect harmony between second causes in their dependance on, and subjection to, the one infinite, wise, good, holy, and just God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-15.htm
- **Matthew Henry (Concise):** The Spirit of life, the Spirit of God, directs all creatures, in heaven and on earth, so as to make them serve the Divine purpose. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-14.htm
- **NET note:** "Spirit" could also be translated "wind." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=10

**v. 18:**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The chariot throne was, as it were, ready for its kingly Rider. From then on, the temple was for Ezekiel what Shiloh had been, a place God had left. It also recalls the voice Josephus reports before the second temple fell: "Let us depart hence." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-18.htm
- **JFB:** Successive steps are marked in His departure; so slowly and reluctantly does the merciful God leave His house. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-18.htm
- **Calvin:** God left, but the temple stayed holy because it rested on his promise. That is why Daniel still prayed toward it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/10-18.html
- **Constable:** God would not share his house with other "gods." The Jerusalem temple faced the same fate as Shiloh. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/10-18.html

**v. 19:**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The gate in view is the outer east gate, the main entrance to the whole temple area. Calling him "God of Israel" shows the covenant God withdrawing his gracious presence from rebellious Jerusalem, though not from the whole nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-18.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** observe with how many stops and pauses God departs, as loth to go, as if to see if there be any that will intercede with him to return. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/10-18.html
- **Guzik:** Ezekiel's wording is ironic, even tragic: the God *of Israel* is leaving Israel. When the glory returns, it comes back through the east gate (43:4). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-10.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The journey pauses here. Even when the vision ends, the glory has gone no further than the Mount of Olives (11:23). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-20.htm

**v. 20:**
- **Cambridge Bible:** It's hard to say how Ezekiel "knew" they were cherubim. It was probably this third sighting, with all its details and movements, that made it clear to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-20.htm
- **Poole:** He knew either by special prophetic assurance or by comparing them with what he had seen in the temple as a priest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-20.htm
- **Clarke:** The people thought the prophets exaggerated, trusting that God's promises to the patriarchs would protect them forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-10.html

**v. 21:**
- **Calvin:** The repetition is there because Ezekiel was speaking to a dull and perverse people who were quick to belittle prophets. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-10.html

**v. 22:**
- **Guzik, quoting Feinberg:** Each creature going straight ahead proclaims the impossibility of thwarting or frustrating the plans of God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-10.cfm
- **Calvin:** Ezekiel recognizes the same God he saw at the river Kebar. This answers people who said he was only offering his own inventions. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-10.html

---

## 2. Where individual teachers differ

- **Who is the man in linen (v. 2)?**
  - **Poole (Puritan, Reformed):** He is Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-2.htm
  - **Gill (Baptist):** In this verse he represents the Chaldean or Roman army. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-2.htm
  - **Guzik (Calvary Chapel):** He is an angel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-10/
- **Reading the wheels as the church (Gill, Baptist):**
  - Gill reads them allegorically: the wheels are The churches by the ministers, with each church having its own pastor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-9.htm
  - He sees the four sides as the steady walk of gospel churches (v. 11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-11.htm
  - **Calvin (Reformed) and JFB** read the wheels as God's providence instead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-10.html
- **Predestination (v. 13):** **Adam Clarke (Methodist)** mocks a preacher who built the doctrine of eternal predestination on "O wheel." But such working of God's word cannot be too severely reprehended. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-10.html
- **Christ as "the God of Israel" (v. 20):**
  - **Gill:** Since the Father never appeared in human form, the figure on the throne is Christ, so this verse is a proof of the true and proper deity of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-20.htm
  - **Poole** reaches the same conclusion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-20.htm
- **The east gate and the future (v. 19):** **Precept Austin**, a dispensational site, reads the route the glory takes as the route of its future return in the millennial kingdom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1015-22

---

## 3. Modern scholarship

- **Cambridge Bible:**
  - The Greek Old Testament (LXX) leaves out v. 14, and the verse is difficult. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-14.htm
  - The chariot description looks artificial to modern readers. The safest course is to admit we don't fully grasp why it mattered so much to Ezekiel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/10-20.htm
- **NET notes:**
  - "Along with their entire bodies" (v. 12) is missing from the LXX and may be a later explanation added to the text.
  - Some English versions (NAB, NLT, TEV, CEV) put "ox" or "bull" in v. 14 to match 1:10, which v. 22 may justify.
  - https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=10
